content_chunks.text: The brain's response to injury includes the activation of intrinsic microglia and the influx of leukocytes, collectively constituting neuroinflammation, the "flame" of the brain. Although details differ and matter, neuroinflammation exacerbating neurodegeneration has similarities across multiple sclerosis and other neurological disorders, such as stroke and neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, lessons from successful disease-modifying therapies in multiple sclerosis may provide insights into strategies for modulating neuroinflammation and reducing neural injury in other neurological conditions. In this Review, we discuss these lessons and potential strategies for counteracting neuroinflammation, including taming the microglia-orchestrated brain immune responses that contribute to progressing neuropathology.

FULL STORY

Researchers at Loma Linda University Health report that eating eggs may be linked to a lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in adults age 65 and older. Their findings suggest that regular egg consumption could play a role in supporting long-term brain health.

The study found that people who ate at least one egg per day for five or more days each week had up to a 27% lower risk of being diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. "Compared to never eating eggs, eating at least five eggs per week can decrease risk of Alzheimer's," said Joan Sabaté, MD, DrPH, a professor at Loma Linda University School of Public Health and the study's principal investigator. Even smaller amounts of egg consumption were associated with benefits. Eating eggs just 1 to 3 times per month was linked to a 17% reduction in risk, while those who ate eggs 2 to 4 times per week saw about a 20% lower risk, Sabaté said. The research, titled Egg intake and the incidence of Alzheimer's disease in the Adventist Health Study-2 cohort linked with Medicare data, was published in the

Journal of Nutrition

. Scientists conducted the study to better understand how diet, a factor people can change, might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's disease.

of Nutrition . Scientists conducted the study to better understand how diet, a factor people can change, might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's disease. Nutrients in Eggs May Support Brain Health

Eggs contain several nutrients that are important for the brain, Sabaté said. They are a rich source of choline, which the body uses to produce compounds such as acetylcholine and phosphatidylcholine that are essential for memory and communication between brain cells. Eggs also provide lutein and zeaxanthin, which are carotenoids that build up in brain tissue and have been linked to better cognitive performance and lower levels of oxidative stress. In addition, eggs contain omega-3 fatty acids, and the yolk is especially high in phospholipids, making up nearly 30% of total egg lipids. These compounds play a key role in how neurotransmitter receptors function. Large Study Tracks Egg Intake and Alzheimer's Diagnoses

To assess egg consumption, researchers considered both direct and indirect sources. This included eggs eaten on their own in forms such as scrambled, fried, or boiled, as well as eggs found in foods like baked goods and packaged products. The study followed about 40,000 participants in the Adventist Health Study 2 cohort.

Alzheimer's cases were identified through physician diagnoses recorded in Medicare data. Eligibility was determined using the Medicare Master Beneficiary Summary Files, and participants were followed for an average of 15.3 years. Balanced Diet Still Key, Researchers Say

The research team stressed that eggs should be part of an overall healthy eating pattern rather than viewed in isolation. "Research supports eggs as part of a healthy diet," said Jisoo Oh, DrPH, MPH, an associate professor of epidemiology at Loma Linda University School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "Seventh-day Adventists do eat a healthier diet than the general public, and we want people to focus on overall health along with this knowledge about the benefit of eggs."

Graduation Goggles Are Real and Need to Be Discussed

The fascinating way your brain puts a positive spin on memories! Nawaf Alsudayri

3 min read

·

--

On a scorching Thursday afternoon, I had some time to spare for myself and decided to use it to revisit one of my favorite shows, How I Met Your Mother. Despite it starting off as an innocent and mindless viewing of the sixth season, my interest was piqued when the show half-heartedly brought up the topic of “Graduation Goggles”. It was at that point when I came to the pretty unfortunate realization that one of psychology’s most interesting theories is best represented in a 2000s sitcom. Now, what exactly are “Graduation Goggles”? At first glance you’d think of them as an accessory to celebrate a person’s big day, but in reality they’re what said person sees when graduating.

first glance you’d think of them as an accessory to celebrate a person’s big day, but in reality they’re what said person sees when graduating. All the people you’ve dreaded waking up to see, the ones you’ve never spoken to, and the professors that have tormented you, all suddenly seem like they’ve been such a huge part of your life, and the thought of that cycle ending, and never seeing any of them again has added a melancholic twist to an otherwise happy day! This point of view is applicable to many scenarios in life – moving apartments, jobs, or even rooms – which is why it has been given its name, however modern psychology attributes it to being applicable to your relationships with others as well, which is why this is the perfect opportunity to raise awareness about Graduation Goggles. A study conducted by Florida State University

has found that in an abusive – or otherwise unhealthy – relationship, the victim mostly returns to their abuser out of love. The belief that the person they have fallen in love with is still there, and is a source of safety to them, making it hard to leave.

that the person they have fallen in love with is still there, and is a source of safety to them, making it hard to leave. This can be linked to a multitude of factors, but I believe there are two key reasons that abusive relationships and friendships can be related to and are shared by Graduation Goggles. The human mind’s love for a routine, and refusal to come to terms with moving on. For so long, we’ve taken this topic as comedy, or a simple metaphor, but I believe Graduation Goggles are a large explanation of many of our problems, and a frequent occurrence that deserves to have a new light shed on it. I can link my experience involving Graduation Goggles with many of my past friendships. In an age in which manipulation has way too many forms, it’s more important now than ever to take off those glasses. The thought of leaving these so-called “friends” who have used me for their own good was a logical thing to do, yet every time I came close to clicking the block button, a rose-tinted splash of all the good memories is the first thing that my mind can formulate.

It’s a neurological phenomenon, which is why it makes it all the weirder when it happens in situations where you and I both know the logical thing to do by a landslide is start a new chapter. It does have an upside to it though! After all, it’s good to leave situations with a high opinion of everything you learned experiencing them, and Graduation Goggles does help massively in doing that, as well as providing emotional closure before inevitably moving on. The fine line people – myself included – cross way too often, is refusing to take them off. It’s nice to look back on an era of your life and look at it with maturity and gratitude as opposed to fear and disdain. The lesson I hope our society learns is that when looking back, we make sure our eyesight is good enough not to need these goggles.
